author: rpvilo
body:
Adds `environment: npm-publish` to the release job, so a human must approve the run in the Actions UI before it can publish.

## Why

Now that the repo is public and publishing uses OIDC, there is no stored npm credential — which is good for secret hygiene, but it means **a push to `main` can reach the registry on its own**. "Who can push to `main`" had become "who can publish `@intentface/chat`".

Two controls close that, and this PR is the second half:

1. **A ruleset on `main`** (already applied, no code): requires a PR, requires `verify` to pass, blocks force-pushes and deletion.
2. **This** — an approval gate immediately before the publish job runs.

## The environment

Configured outside this PR, via the API:

- **Name:** `npm-publish`
- **Required reviewer:** `rpvilo` (self-review permitted, since it's a single reviewer)
- **Branch policy:** `main` only

Effect: the release job sits in "Waiting" until approved. It's the same proof-of-presence property as npm's staged publishing, but it works today — `npm stage` needs CLI 11.15.0 and we're on 11.13.0.

## Worth knowing

The gate covers the **whole job**, not just the publish step. So when the workflow is only opening or updating a Version Packages PR, it also waits for approval. That's one extra click per release cycle, which seemed a fair trade rather than splitting the job in two to distinguish the cases.

Optional tightening, not done here: npm's trusted publisher config accepts an environment name. Setting it to `npm-publish` when you configure the trusted publisher would make npm itself reject an OIDC token minted outside this environment, rather than relying only on GitHub to enforce it.

## Verified

Workflow YAML parses; `environment`, `permissions` and triggers are unchanged apart from the addition. No package code touched, so no changeset.

author: kaaburgh
body:
## Problem

On-device validation on the LG G5 showed the quality switcher had no effect at all. Across three diagnostics captures with different selections, the HLS state was identical:

| selected quality | currentLevel | mode | loading |
|---|---|---|---|
| 720p | 3 | auto | 1606p |
| 480p | 3 | auto | 1606p |
| Авто | 3 | auto | 1606p |

Playback never restarted between switches (buffer ranges and the frame counter ran continuously), which confirms every quality entry resolves to the same `hls4` master playlist — so the in-place level switch is the *only* mechanism that can change quality, and it was not firing.

## Cause

Levels were resolved by exact `level.height` equality against the API quality name. That only holds for 16:9 content. The stream in the captures is a 2.39:1 encode, and its `available` line reads:

```
302p / 0.3 Mbps, 536p / 0.5 Mbps, 804p / 0.8 Mbps, 1606p / 2.1 Mbps
```

i.e. 854x302 / 1280x536 / 1920x804 / 3840x1606 for what the API calls 480p / 720p / 1080p / 2160p. `findIndex((l) => l.height === targetHeight)` therefore always returned `-1`, `currentLevel` was never set, and hls.js silently stayed in its default ABR mode — which is also why `mode` read `auto` even with a fixed quality selected, and why every selection played back identically at the top level.

This predates the Auto/Fixed work (#2); that PR made it legible by surfacing `selected quality` next to the hls.js-derived `mode`.

## Fix

Normalize each level to the quality it actually represents — the larger of its advertised height and the 16:9-equivalent height implied by its width — and match nearest-first so a fixed choice always lands on a deterministic level:

| level | normalized |
|---|---|
| 854x302 | 480p |
| 1280x536 | 720p |
| 1920x804 | 1080p |
| 3840x1606 | 2160p |

`max(height, width * 9/16)` keeps 16:9 exact (1280x720 → 720) and leaves taller-than-16:9 content on its real height (640x480 → 480). When a manifest omits `RESOLUTION`, it falls back to height alone. Nearest-first matching replaces exact equality so a selection is never silently dropped.

The diagnostics level list now shows both the normalized name and the real resolution (`1080p (1920x804) / 0.8 Mbps`), so this class of mismatch is readable straight off the overlay.

## Test plan

- [x] `npx tsc --noEmit` — clean
- [x] `yarn eslint` — clean
- [x] Mapping verified against the exact level sets from the captures, plus 16:9, 4:3, missing-width, and empty/invalid-name cases
- [ ] On-device re-check on the LG G5: switching between 480p/720p/1080p/2160p should move `currentLevel` and flip `mode` to `fixed`, and `Авто` should keep `mode: auto`

Note for the on-device pass: capture #3 also shows `buffer starvation: 2` while `bandwidthEstimate` was 39.7 Mbps against a 2.1 Mbps top level — unrelated to this fix, and relevant evidence for roadmap items 1 and 4.

author: plantucha
body:
`OXYDEX-PULSE-RESOURCING-FOLLOWUPS` §3 asked for the **measured** agreement between the O2Ring's 1 Hz vendor pulse and an HR derived from its own finger PPG. Two earlier passes failed; the second left it open and correctly refused to quote a bias.

## The blocker was one line of file selection

The ring writes one `_SPO2.csv` per `_PPG.txt`, sharing a 14-digit session stamp:

```
Wellue_O2Ring-S_S8AW2100_20260727001113_PPG.txt
Wellue_O2Ring-S_S8AW2100_20260727001113_SPO2.csv
```

Pass 2 took `find … _SPO2.csv | head -1` (an arbitrary session) against the **largest** `_PPG.txt` (usually a different one), so on almost every night it window-matched two unrelated sessions and correctly found no overlap. Its diagnosis — *"they are different capture sessions on the same date"* — described the symptom of its own file selection. No `trio-batch`-style session inference was needed; **the key was in the filename all along.**

Now paired by stamp and compared **per 5-min epoch** rather than one median per session: `PPGDSP.analyze` already yields `epochs[].hr`, so each epoch is matched against the median vendor pulse over that epoch's own wall-clock window — the paired series a Bland–Altman actually needs.

## Result — 614 paired epochs, 43 sessions, 6 nights

| | |
|---|---|
| bias (ppg − vendor) | **+0.84 bpm** |
| SD | 3.34 bpm |
| 95 % LoA | **−5.72 … +7.39 bpm** |
| median Δ | **0.00 bpm** |
| per-night median Δ | **0.00 on all six nights** (n 19/163/134/103/99/96) |

The **legitimate negative result** §3 allowed for — it corroborates the synthetic's Δ≈2 and the parent §7's *"vendor smoothing costs little"*, measured this time. Per-night medians are printed beside the pooled figure precisely so a bias dominated by one night would be visible; it isn't.

**The `--min-cov` inclusion rule does not drive it:** at 0.25 / 0.50 / 0.75 the answer is bias **0.82 / 0.84 / 0.83**, SD 3.35 / 3.34 / 3.37 (n 632 / 614 / 601). A threshold nobody varied is an invented constant.

## A silent drop found on the way — and it had produced a plausible answer

The first complete run reported **155 epochs / 5 nights / bias 0.80 / SD 2.00**. Wrong: the **seven largest sessions** (the actual overnight recordings, 92–142 MB) were being counted `analyse failed`. The child wrote ~500 KB of JSON with `process.stdout.write` then `process.exit(0)`; stdout to a **pipe** is async, so every payload truncated at exactly **146176 bytes** and the parent's `JSON.parse` failed. Nothing errored — the run just summarised the short reconnect fragments and printed a *tighter, healthier-looking* SD.

Two things make it worth recording:
- **It reproduces only through a pipe.** A file redirect writes synchronously and looks fine — which is how my earlier spot-check passed.
- **Removing the `exit()` is not the fix.** The vm realm keeps the event loop alive and the child hangs. The fix is a synchronous `writeSync(1, …)` loop over partial writes, then a deliberate exit.

Shipped run: **0 analyse failures.**

## Gates

node lane **5309 green** · docs-ledger 22/22 · release-ledger 9/9 · GATE A 9/9 + GATE B · all three build systems clean (tool-only change, no bundle impact) · biome clean.

Brief flipped **DONE** — §1 measured NO 2026-07-21, §2 re-stamped, §3 now answered.

- **Real measurement** against the actual private one-hop working set (methodology public in `docs/GRAPH_BENCHMARK_METHOD.md`; real byte/timing figures in `local/benchmarks/`, never committed, per ADR 0018): the 140-album catalog's 1-hop ego network compresses smaller than the largest artifact already shipped (`routes/rounds.v1.json`, 2.9MB), with fast parse/BFS even under simulated low-end-mobile CPU throttling (via Playwright + CDP `Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate`). A 500-album tier's 1-hop network is measurably larger but plausible; its 2-hop network balloons an order of magnitude and already touches most of the entire corpus's edges.
- **ADR 0050**: browser-local CSR search is viable at a small bounded scope (roughly 140-500 albums), not the full one-hop corpus or an unrestricted multi-hop expansion from a large seed set. DuckDB-WASM and a bounded Cloudflare Worker remain legitimate fallbacks, explicitly not measured in this pass since the evidence didn't require them yet.

author: hemendra1315
body:
## Summary

Batches: create/edit/soft-delete, a detail page, coach assignment and player add/remove. Based on the Phase 2 branch (PR #1) because it needs the `players`/`coaches` tables; no training sessions, schedules or attendance yet. Migrations `0007`–`0010` are already applied to the hosted project and recorded in `schema_migrations`.

**Batch membership is now the answer to the Phase 2 gap** ("coach sees assigned players" was unenforceable without an assignment table). `0008` tightens the policy:

```sql
-- before: is_staff(academy_id) -> a coach saw every player in the academy
create policy players_select on players for select using (
  is_owner(academy_id) or user_id = auth.uid()
  or shares_batch_with_player(id)   -- coach shares an active batch with them
  or is_super_admin()
);
```

`venues`/`batches`/`batch_coaches`/`batch_players` are readable by any member and writable by owners only. `batch_players` read is narrower: owner, a coach on that batch, or the player themselves.

**Anything multi-row goes through an RPC** (`0009`) so a capacity check cannot race its own insert, and so a delete cannot half-apply:

```sql
add_players_to_batch(batch, players[]) -> int   -- skips duplicates, raises E_BATCH_FULL
                                                -- locks the batch row, counts only left_at is null
remove_player_from_batch(batch, player)         -- stamps left_at; history is kept
assign_player_to_batches(player, batches[])     -- the API-plan entry point: leaves unlisted batches
assign_coach_to_batch(batch, coach, is_primary) -- demotes the previous primary first, since
                                                -- batch_coaches_primary_idx is unique where is_primary
delete_batch(batch)                             -- releases roster + detaches coaches + soft-deletes
```

Cross-tenant references are rejected in the database rather than trusted from the client: triggers assert that a batch's `venue_id`, and every `batch_coaches`/`batch_players` row's person, share the row's `academy_id` (`E_VENUE_OTHER_ACADEMY`, `E_CROSS_ACADEMY`). All new `E_*` identifiers are translated in `errors.ts`.

Roster counts come from aggregate embeds so the list stays one request, with the filter applied to the embedded table so released players aren't counted:

```ts
.select('…, venues(name), batch_players(count), batch_coaches(count)')
.is('batch_players.left_at', null)
```

The form keeps numbers as strings (the established `optionalInteger` pattern) and converts once in `toBatchInput`, which also turns the rupee fee into `monthly_fee_paise`.

### Review follow-ups (second commit)

Three small defects found while reviewing, none of them refactors:

- `created_by` was silently null on every batch, because the row is inserted from the client — `0010` gives it `default auth.uid()`.
- `unique (academy_id, name)` also covered soft-deleted rows, so deleting a batch permanently reserved its name; it is now a partial unique index `where deleted_at is null`.
- A duplicate name surfaced the raw Postgres text (`duplicate key value violates unique constraint "batches_…"`) because `errorMessage` had no `CONFLICT`/`VALIDATION` case — the same class of leak fixed in Phase 1.
- `batches:read` was missing from the player role, so a player could reach `/batches` by URL but never saw the nav entry; RLS already scopes the rows they can read.

## Verification

`npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint` (0 warnings), 43 unit tests, `npm run build` — all pass.

Exercised against the hosted project through real PostgREST calls with a signed-in owner JWT, and via impersonated roles in SQL, then rolled back (DB is back to one academy, one member, zero players):

- primary-coach uniqueness and primary swap; capacity refusal at the limit; duplicate add returning `0`; a cross-academy player failing to join
- a coach seeing exactly their 2 batch players and being refused a roster write (`E_FORBIDDEN`); an unrelated user seeing zero batch/venue rows
- the aggregate-count query specifically: a batch with no players is still listed with `count 0`, and a released (`left_at`) player is excluded
- `assign_player_to_batches(player, '{}')` releasing every batch, and `delete_batch` leaving no active roster rows or coach links

## Not covered

No browser testing of these screens yet — it needs a Google sign-in. Venues have a table, RLS and a batch picker, but no CRUD screen; there is no way to create one from the UI yet.

author: jason-te-sde
body:
## What

Snapshots and log compaction, paper section 7: the state machine can be serialized, the
log prefix discarded, and a follower that has fallen too far behind caught up from a
snapshot instead of from entries. Works in the simulator and over gRPC.

## Why

Without it the log grows forever, a restart replays from index 1, and a follower that
falls behind the leader's oldest retained entry can never be repaired, because the
entries it needs no longer exist. This was the largest gap in v0.1.0.

## The split

The core's part is narrow on purpose: it decides **when** a follower needs a snapshot and
**which boundary** that snapshot establishes. It does not move bytes, because it has no
I/O. So `RaftMessage.InstallSnapshot` carries metadata only, and the transport streams the
payload on its own RPC whose **response means installed, not received** — a leader must not
learn a follower holds a snapshot before the follower holds it.

## Ordering is where the safety lives

Three places, all of which can lose committed data if reversed:

1. The state machine snapshot is written and fsynced **before** the log is compacted.
   Compaction is the point of no return.
2. A received snapshot is durable and checksum-verified **before** the core is told about it.
3. A snapshot in a `Ready` batch is installed **before** that batch's entries are appended,
   because those entries sit above its boundary. This one is now written into the `Ready`
   contract, because it is not obvious and I got it wrong first.

Startup refuses to run if the log claims a boundary no snapshot covers. The entries below it
are gone and so is their effect; starting anyway would hide data loss rather than report it.

## Testing

206 tests, green on JDK 21 and 25.

The simulator now compacts during every run: `SimConfig` presets use thresholds of 8 to 16
entries, which is deliberately unrealistic so that every seed crosses the paths a production
threshold would reach once an hour. The soak test asserts snapshots actually happened, since
a sweep where nothing compacted would leave all of this untested.

Integration tests on real sockets:

- `followerCatchesUpFromASnapshot` — stop a follower, write 60 keys so the leader compacts,
  restart it, and assert it is repaired *and* that it was repaired by a snapshot rather than
  by entries
- `restartsFromItsOwnSnapshot` — a node whose own log no longer contains the early entries
  still comes back with those keys, which is only possible via its snapshot file

## Four bugs this surfaced

Worth listing, because they are all the same shape — "the log no longer starts at index 1":

1. **Log Matching compared by list position.** Two nodes that compacted at different points
   have durable logs starting at different indexes, so the checker was comparing index 5 on
   one node against index 1 on another and reporting a violation. Now compared by log index
   over the overlapping range only.
2. **A follower treated already-committed entries as conflicts.** With `prevLogIndex` below
   its snapshot boundary it could not verify the match, called it a conflict, and refused
   because the index was at or below its commit index. It now points the leader at its
   boundary instead.
3. **A compaction marker discarded entries above its own boundary** during replay, so every
   restart after a compaction silently lost the log tail. Found by a storage test.
4. **The simulator paired snapshot payloads with the wrong metadata**, because they were keyed
   by recipient alone and two leaders can have snapshots in flight to the same node at
   different boundaries. It presented as a compaction request past the end of the log several
   hundred ticks later, which is exactly the kind of delayed, confusing failure the seeded
   simulator makes tractable.

Also worth noting: adding the two messages to the sealed `RaftMessage` interface broke the
codec's compilation immediately, which is the guarantee that design was bought for.

## Notes for the reviewer

- Snapshot payloads are held whole in memory when sent and received. Fine for the key spaces
  this handles; a store with a large state machine would want to stream from disk to socket
  without buffering, and the chunking is already in place for that.
- Older snapshots are kept (three of them) rather than deleted immediately. They cost disk and
  buy a fallback if the newest one fails its checksum.
- `receivedSnapshot` is a single field, so one snapshot can be in flight to a node at a time.
  A second concurrent stream would overwrite it. The leader only ever has one outstanding per
  follower, but that is an assumption the field should not have to make.

Closes #3

author: sykk
body:
Closes #380. Second outside-the-record probe, and this one found a defect that
fires on every reconnect.

Nothing in `docs/manual-verification.md` covered unread across a reconnect, so I
went looking at the seam between session state and history replay.

**A gap fill hands back the last message you read, and the badge counted it.**

```text
live message, msgid=abc          unread 1
mark_read                        unread 0
gap fill returns
  msgid=abc (already read)
  msgid=def (genuinely missed)   unread 2   ← 1 was right
```

The overlap is created on purpose. `history::at` truncates the resume timestamp
to the milliseconds the format carries, and its comment gives the cost:

> Truncating the sub-second part moves the bound earlier, which at worst asks
> again for a message already held — the archive refuses the duplicate.

The archive does refuse it — #335 built that. The unread count never did.
`close_batch` counted a replayed message whenever it filled a gap and the sender
was in the conversation, and nothing asked whether the reader already had it.

It bites on **every** reconnect where a conversation's newest message was
stamped by this machine rather than the server — `archived` keeps nanoseconds
and the resume carries milliseconds — and on any server that includes the
boundary message in its own answer.

**The fix** measures a replayed message against the watermark its conversation
held *before* the batch began, rather than the running one the loop moves
forward as it goes. Strictly newer, which cuts the other way: a genuinely missed
message sharing the exact server timestamp of the last one read is drawn and not
counted. That is a millisecond collision against a badge that was wrong on every
reconnect, and the code states the trade rather than hiding it.

Two tests added — the overlap, and a page of nothing new leaving the badge alone
— and the five that were already in `what_a_backfill_counts` still pass, which
is what says the first-page rule and the service-narration rule are untouched.

Still no evidence for the badge against a real socket. That was already recorded
and this does not change it.

author: saud-alnasser
body:
Closes #219

Stacked: first of four, based on `main`.

## 🎯 Changes

Records what the interface costs today, so the interface overhaul (#211) has before-numbers to be checked against. ADR 0009 replaces the list block for all five lists at once, so these become unrecoverable the moment that lands.

Adds one file, `.claude/evidence/research/interface-performance-baseline.md`. **No application code is touched.**

Measured against a seeded database at two absolute scales — 400 and 5,000 tenants — driving the real routers through the real tRPC caller over a query-counting transport, plus a real browser scrolling the real application with every blurred surface in place.

**What the numbers say**

- **The contract list scans whole tables in TypeScript on every keystroke.** 27.8 ms and 1.52 MB across the IPC boundary per keystroke at 4,423 contracts, against 0.56 ms and 2.7 kB for a list that filters in SQL. The cost does not depend on the search term — it loads everything regardless.
- **Reconcile is linear in table size, not in what the mutation touched.** 2.6 ms → 40.7 ms across the two scales, 184 kB → 2.63 MB. Four unbounded reads on every mutation *and* at every application start, where it measured 75 ms.
- **No paginated list's query count grows with the rows it renders** — a fixed 1, 2 or 3 per page, and the tenth page costs the same as the first.
- **Scrolling is not the problem, and the blur is not what costs when there is one.** Every list holds vsync at 5.9 ms/frame with 26–90 live `backdrop-filter` surfaces. Under 6× CPU throttling frames do blow the budget, but removing every blur did not improve them in any condition measured.

**Two findings contradict premises the overhaul was planned on.** Both are recorded, neither is fixed here:

- `data-table.svelte` renders no list — corrected by #222, dead code deleted by #225.
- The blur's cost is a compositing claim, not a measured frame cost. "Zero blurred surfaces" stands on the aesthetic argument, not the performance one.

Both harnesses were Position code and were deleted; the file describes the method closely enough to rebuild, and says so in its Limitations.

## ✅ Checklist

- [ ] I have added or updated the tests related to the changes made.

No test surface — this adds a documentation file and changes no executable code. The suite was green at the time of writing (220 pass, 0 fail).

author: sslivins
body:
## Summary
Fixes a serious OTA bug that **bricked the running app** and reverted a device to the old factory image.

## Symptom
After triggering a firmware update, a device ended up running the old **v1.1.0 'ESP32 PoE Temperature Monitor'** firmware (from before this repo was renamed to thermux).

## Root cause
`ota_updater.c` selected the firmware asset by taking the **first** release asset whose name merely *contains* `.bin`. thermux releases publish **three** `.bin` assets — `bootloader.bin`, `partition-table.bin`, `thermux.bin` — so it picked **bootloader.bin**. Writing the bootloader image into the app OTA slot corrupts the app; on reboot the second-stage bootloader falls back to the **factory partition** (the old 1.1.0 image).

## Fix
- Select the **exact app asset** `<repo>.bin` (e.g. `thermux.bin`), explicitly skipping `bootloader.bin` / `partition-table.bin`, with a safe fallback to any other `.bin`.
- If no download URL resolves, mark no update available and **abort the update task** instead of flashing a bad/empty URL.
- Bump `APP_VERSION` to **2.8.3**.

## Testing
- Reproduced live: a device fell back to 1.1.0 after an update; recovered via the direct `/api/ota/upload` path.
- Firmware compilation validated by CI (ESP-IDF Build).
- Post-merge: release v2.8.3, flash the device via direct upload (its running 2.8.2 still has the bug), then verify the **GitHub OTA / HA update entity** install path now pulls `thermux.bin` and lands on the correct version.

nicht angefasst**. Eine Assertion gegen das gerenderte HTML bricht den Lauf ab, statt ein
Bild mit einem Originalwert zu schreiben; zusätzlich wurde jedes der acht PNGs einzeln
gesichtet.

- Alle relativen Links und Bildpfade in beiden READMEs aufgelöst (kein 404 auf GitHub)

## Hinweis zur History

Der Tailnet-FQDN steckt zusätzlich in zwei alten Commits (`97cd3a4`, `360f3f1`). Die
History wurde **bewusst nicht** umgeschrieben: ein Tailnet-Hostname ist kein Credential
(außerhalb des Tailnets weder auflösbar noch erreichbar), während ein `filter-repo` +
Force-Push alle nachfolgenden SHAs ändern, die `GIT_SHA`-Self-Update-Prüfung der laufenden
Instanz ins Leere laufen lassen und sämtliche PR-Referenzen entwerten würde.

author: saud-alnasser
body:
Closes #220

Stacked: second of four, on top of #226.

## 🎯 Changes

ADR 0007 settled that shadcn-svelte's Rhea style is this rebuild's density target and that it is transcribed by hand, because the documented adoption path — `init --reinstall` — is the one operation that silently strips the i18n and RTL wiring from more than thirty primitive files. What the ADR does not carry is the actual scale. This is it.

Adds one file, `.claude/evidence/research/rhea-geometry-scale.md`. **No file under `src/` is modified, and no CLI was run** — the registry was read over HTTP, so nothing could touch `src/lib/design/primitive/`.

All 56 of Rhea's `registry:ui` items were fetched and diffed against their default-style counterparts. The scale covers control heights, spacing steps, the type scale, radius, and how borders and surfaces are treated, with a source link per group and a pixel value beside every token.

**Rhea is a control-density and radius change, not a table one.** Its table geometry *is* the default's. Density comes from controls dropping a step — button `h-9`→`h-8`, select trigger `h-9`→`h-7`, toggle `h-10`→`h-7` — a new `xs` step, and radius moving up. Against the primitives here that is **8px off every control height**.

**Three deviations are required rather than optional, and each fails silently if the class strings are copied verbatim:**

1. **Rhea is written LTR.** 138 physical direction utilities against 30 logical, where the default style this repository generated from is 4 against 123 — across 31 of 56 families. Porting verbatim would *regress* the RTL support that exists today.
2. **Its selectors target a newer Bits UI attribute contract.** Rhea uses `data-checked:` / `data-open:`; bits-ui 2.18.1 emits `data-state`, and no file in its `dist` emits a bare `data-checked` at all. A checked checkbox would render unchecked with nothing erroring. Rhea declares `bits-ui@^2.16.3`, which 2.18.1 satisfies — so the declared range is not the guard.
3. **The radius ladder inverts here.** `app.css` overrides `--radius-xl` to 18px while `--radius-2xl` falls through to Tailwind's 16px, so `rounded-xl` > `rounded-2xl`. Rhea assumes the opposite, so every menu item would be more rounded than the menu holding it. Two remaps are stated and neither is chosen — that is a Decision, and it belongs to the ticket that applies the palette.

Also confirms ADR 0007's rejected variable-only option from the source: Rhea's index carries 56 UI items and **no** `registry:style` or `registry:theme` item, so there are no CSS variables to adopt.

The registry is unversioned, so the file pins what it can — the served date, the repo SHA, and CLI `shadcn-svelte@1.5.0` — and says in Limitations that nothing pins the registry itself.

## ✅ Checklist

- [ ] I have added or updated the tests related to the changes made.

No test surface — this adds a documentation file and changes no executable code.

author: raphaeltimbo
body:
## Summary

This PR replaces the finite-difference `fluid_flow` bearing engine with a new thermo-elasto-hydrodynamic (TEHD) finite-element solver for fluid-film journal bearings, and rebuilds the user-facing bearing classes on top of it.

### New internal solver (`ross/bearings/fluid_film`)

A self-contained TEHD FE engine for fixed-geometry and tilting-pad journal bearings:

- Generalized Reynolds equation with cross-film viscosity variation and turbulence (Safar & Szeri; Reichardt wall law)
- Adiabatic and full (conducting-pad) energy equations
- Pad elastic and thermal deformation; four pivot-flexibility models (Hertzian ball/button/rocker contact and user stiffness)
- Starved, axial-flow and high-ambient-pressure operation; pressure-dam and tapered-land geometry
- Dynamic-coefficient reduction over the pad tilt and pivot degrees of freedom
- SI in, SI out; numba-accelerated inner kernels (`cache=True`)

26 self-contained `{inputs, outputs}` regression fixtures span the solver's control space and are pinned at rtol 1e-8 (the two slowest gated behind `ROSS_FLUID_FILM_SLOW=1`).

### New element classes

- **`FluidFilmBearing(BearingElement)`** — connects the solver to the element interface: lubricant resolution from `lubricants_dict`, one solver case per frequency (serial or `num_processes` multiprocessing), synchronous 2x2 coefficient table for the rotor assembly, interpolating `coefficients(frequency)`, and `save()`/`load()` that round-trips a plain coefficient table so loading never re-runs the solver. Opt-in `field_outputs` expose pressure, film-thickness and film-temperature grids, plotted through `FluidFilmBearingResults` (per-pad 3-D surfaces, center-plane profiles, summary and coefficient tables).
- **Fixed-geometry configuration classes** — `FixedGeometryBearing` plus `PartialArcBearing`, `EllipticalBearing`, `OffsetHalvesBearing`, `MultiLobeBearing` and `PressureDamBearing` (Nicholas & Allaire), each translating the classic geometry into the solver's per-pad arrays.
- **`PlainJournal` and `TiltingPad` rewritten** on the engine, keeping their historical constructor surfaces. Retired knobs are accepted with deprecation warnings; new capabilities (pivot flexibility, leading-edge-groove and spray-bar lubrication, pad deformation, load-matched equilibrium) come along for free.

### Validation against the literature

- **Lund & Thomsen (1978)**: two-axial-groove (L/D 0.5 and 1) and elliptical (preload 0.5) tables — eccentricity, attitude angle and all eight dimensionless coefficients within 6 % (observed 1–3 %)
- **Nicholas, Barrett & Leader (1980)**: step journal bearings — Sommerfeld, eccentricity, rigid-rotor stability parameter within 8 %, plus dimensional coefficient tables; two-axial-groove stability baseline within 1 %
- **Fillon et al. (1992)**: 4-pad LBP tilting pad at 10 kN — peak pad temperature within 3.5 °C of the paper's TEHD prediction over 1000–4000 rpm

The literature work also exposed and fixed a `threshold_rpm` unit error (value stored in rad/s under the rpm-named key).

### Breaking changes (see the 2.4.0 release notes / migration guide)

- The `fluid_flow` subpackage, `BearingFluidFlow` and `ST_BearingElement.from_fluid_flow` are removed
- `PlainJournalResults` / `TiltingPadResults` are replaced by `FluidFilmBearingResults`
- `PlainJournal` results differ numerically from previous versions (different turbulence model, cavitation treatment and energy equation); the `method` split (`lund`/`perturbation`, which disagreed by ~2x on kyy) is gone

### Docs

2.4.0 release notes with a migration guide, rewritten advanced-bearings cookbook, regenerated bearings tutorial, API reference for the new family, and removal of the `fluid_flow` notebooks.

## Test plan

- `pytest ross/tests/test_fluid_film_solver.py` — 26 pinned solver fixtures at rtol 1e-8
- `pytest ross/tests/test_fluid_film_bearing.py ross/tests/test_fixed_geometry.py` — element construction reproduces raw solver fixtures at rtol 1e-8; parallel equals serial bit-for-bit; save/load round-trip; geometry translation per configuration class
- `pytest ross/tests/test_fluid_film_literature.py` — the literature cases above
- Existing `PlainJournal`/`TiltingPad` suites rewritten as translation-equivalence tests
- `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` pass

## What

Implements catalog query and routing commands: `dt catalog resolve`, `get`, `deps`, `consumers`, `flow`, `closure`, and `coverage`.

## Why

Refs #46
Closes #46

## How

- `core/catalog/resolve.ts` — text normalization (lowercase, de-accent, light es/en stemming, stopword removal) + weighted lexical scorer (exact id, alias, flow alias, domain, description) with default threshold 20, top 12 results.
- `core/catalog/queries.ts` — graph reads: `get`, `deps` (depth/direction traversal), `consumers`, `flow`, `closure` (transitive dependency closure with dedup and cap).
- `core/catalog/coverage.ts` — extraction quality aggregation per component and per confidence.
- `adapters/cli/catalog-query.ts` + `bin/dt.ts` routing — wires all subcommands under `dt catalog <subcommand>` with `--json` support.

The Cedar authorization layer failed in every direction at once: adding your first policy took the gateway offline, and no policy you wrote ever persisted or took effect. Four defects compounding.

## The first `permit` bricked everything it didn't match

Evaluation was default-deny globally, so:

```
permit(principal, action == Action::"read", resource);
```

— the obvious first policy, and the one the README suggested — 403'd every write endpoint including `POST /api/chat` and `POST /admin/policies`. That last one meant the gateway could not be recovered through its own API, and pre-fix policies didn't survive a restart either.

Deny is now **scoped per action**: an action is *governed* once some `ENFORCE` statement names it (or omits the action clause, thereby covering all of them). Within a governed action Cedar's rules are unchanged — a matching permit is required, and a matching forbid overrides it. An action nobody wrote a rule about falls through to the layers that are always on: authentication, admin RBAC, and quota enforcement.

The alternative — keeping global default-deny and telling operators to write an allow-all policy first — puts the safe configuration one forgotten step away from a self-inflicted outage, and the failure is silent until someone tries to write. The reasoning is in the `CedarPolicyService` docstring, where a reader will find it.

## A single `LOG_ONLY` policy denied every method

`LOG_ONLY` statements `continue`d without setting `permitted`, so under global default-deny the documented way to *safely trial* a policy — and the mode `POST /admin/policies` **defaults to** — was the worst case: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and HEAD all DENY. LOG_ONLY now governs nothing, so it cannot change a decision.

## Policies never persisted and never took effect

`create_policy` had no persistence call, and statements were compiled once at construction — so a policy applied only after a restart it could not survive.

- `save_cedar_policy` / `load_all_cedar_policies` in `persistence.py`, keyed `CEDAR_POLICY#<name>` to match the route's update-by-name identity. Deserialization defaults `mode` to `LOG_ONLY` so a malformed item can't become enforcing.
- `CedarPolicyService.reload()`, building the new lists before swapping them in — an unparseable statement mid-list must not leave a half-built policy set deciding requests.
- Bootstrap builds **one** evaluator and hands the same instance to both `AdminAPI` and `AuthMiddleware`, so a `POST` recompiles the object requests actually consult. It's now constructed unconditionally: the previous `if comp.policies else None` meant a gateway that booted with no policies had no evaluator to recompile, so the first policy an operator added did nothing until a restart.
- Persisted policies load at startup and merge over seeded ones **by name** — evaluating a persisted policy alongside the seeded one it replaces would, for a permit/forbid pair, silently resolve to DENY.

## Scope clauses were silently dropped, widening the statement

Found while verifying the README against a running gateway. `resource == Resource::"/api/chat"` parsed and then forbade *every* write; `principal == User::"alice"` parsed and then permitted *everyone*. Each clause **narrows** a statement, so dropping it **widens** its effect — the same fail-open class as the original bug. These, plus `principal in`, `resource in`, `action in [...]`, and a bare `permit;` with no scope triple (which parsed as "permit everything"), are now rejected — with a **400** from `POST /admin/policies` rather than a log line at startup nobody reads. Construction still tolerates one, so a policy stored before this check can't stop the gateway booting.

The module docstring had claimed `resource == Model::"gpt-4o"` was supported. It never was.

## Verified against a running gateway

Not just unit-tested — the documented workflow was run end to end under `AXON_AUTH_MODE=ENFORCE`:

```
baseline (no policies)     writes: 201  reads: 200
POST LOG_ONLY              -> 201 {'name': 'seniors-write', 'status': 'created'}
  after LOG_ONLY           writes: 201  reads: 200
POST same name, ENFORCE    -> 200 {'name': 'seniors-write', 'status': 'updated'}
  after ENFORCE            writes: 403  reads: 200
unsupported text           -> 400
```

Both documented lockout-recovery routes were confirmed the same way (restart with `AXON_AUTH_MODE=LOG_ONLY`; delete the `CEDAR_POLICY#<name>` item and restart).

## Remaining footgun, documented rather than fixed

An `ENFORCE` `forbid` on `write` can still lock you out of `POST /admin/policies` while `GET` keeps working. That's the policy doing exactly what it says, so it's a `> [!WARNING]` in the README with both verified recovery routes, not a special case in the evaluator.

## Tests

65 tests. New `tests/unit/test_cedar_policy_lifecycle.py` covers the gap between the evaluator tests and the route tests: route → evaluator → persistence, with a `_RecordingPersistence(DynamoPersistence)` subclass so `serialize_cedar_policy` — the part that decides what actually reaches the table — is code under test rather than a fake. `test_bootstrap.py` asserts `is` identity on the shared evaluator and covers the startup load.

Three pre-existing tests asserted the old behaviour; each was **rewritten to assert the new semantics** with an explanatory docstring rather than deleted, so coverage didn't shrink.

Mutation-tested with 25 mutations across all four source files, all caught. Four survivors across two rounds each became a real test — including two I checked with a differential harness first rather than assuming they were equivalent mutants (they weren't: a condition *value* containing `==` or the word `in` distinguishes them).

`ruff check src/ tests/` clean; **2115 passed / 1 skipped**; README 47 headings, 0 broken anchors.

## Note on PR #71

#71's `### Authentication and authorization` section documents the Cedar behaviour this PR changes, including the `permit(… Action::"read" …)` example that was the footgun. Whichever merges second needs its Cedar text reconciled — I'll do that on the branch that lands after.

author: mgiota
body:
## Summary

Fixes #282411.

The Synthetics **bulk edit locations** flyout (added in #279233) posts to the **public** route `PUT /api/synthetics/monitors/_bulk_update`, and `fetchBulkUpdateMonitors` does **not** send `?internal=true`. Without an explicit private-location field, that route's location normalizer (`parseMonitorLocations`) carries a monitor's existing **private** locations forward. As a result, **Overwrite** (and **Remove**) silently re-add a private location the user intended to drop:

- Overwrite 2 monitors that use a private location with a public location → both the public **and** the old private location remain.
- Remove a private location while a public one stays → the private one comes back.

Add mode and public-only monitors are unaffected.

## What changed (Option 1)

In the flyout's `handleSave`, split the authoritative per-monitor set into public `locations` and an explicit `private_locations` id list — **including an empty array when no private location remains** — and always send both. An explicit (even empty) `private_locations` disambiguates the payload so the public API's normalizer takes the set verbatim in every mode.

- `bulk_locations_flyout.tsx`: new `toLocationsPatch` helper; `handleSave` sends `locations` + `private_locations`.
- `state/monitor_list/api.ts`: widen `BulkUpdateMonitorRequest.attributes` to allow the request-only `private_locations?: string[]`.
- Added a regression test: overwriting a private-only monitor with a public location now clears the private location (`private_locations: []`).

## Alternative considered (Option 2)

Pass `internal=true` from the bulk-edit call (mirroring the single-monitor UI edit) so `parseMonitorLocations` treats the array as authoritative. Not taken: it's more invasive (the public versioned route would need a query schema for `internal`) and changes semantics of a public endpoint. Option 1 is smaller and server-behavior-neutral.

## Why QA didn't catch it earlier

The feature-acceptance scenario `bulk-edit-locations-schedule.json` did **not** exercise the bug path:

1. **Wrong mode** — the flyout defaults to **Add**; the scenario never switched to **Overwrite** (or **Remove**).
2. **Never saved** — it clicked **Cancel**, so no bulk update ran.
3. **No post-save screenshot** — there was no after-state capture of the locations column.

A scenario that **switches to Overwrite, saves, and screenshots the monitor list afterward** would have caught this via human review — the gap was **scenario design**, not a limitation of screenshot-based QA. A dedicated overwrite scenario is added in this PR's QA run (see issue #282411 for screenshots).

## Test plan

- [x] `node scripts/jest .../monitor_list_table/bulk_locations_flyout.test.tsx` (10 passing, incl. new regression test)
- [x] eslint clean on changed files
- [x] QA feature-acceptance: `bulk-edit-locations-overwrite.json` — overwrite private → public, post-save locations screenshot
- [x] Manual: create 2 `ui` monitors on a private location → bulk **Edit locations → Overwrite** → pick a public location → Save → both monitors show only the public location.
- [x] Manual: monitor on public + private → bulk **Remove** the private location → monitor keeps only the public location.
- [x] Manual: **Add** mode still unions locations as before.

author: rambleraptor
body:
## Summary

Consolidates every hand-rolled engine REST layer onto the shared
`@rambleraptor/homestead-client` package and deletes the parallel `aepGet` /
`aepList` / `aepCreate` / `aepCreateMultipart` / `aepUpdate` / `aepRemove`
free functions. After this change there is one client library — no bespoke
`fetch` wrapper anywhere.

Two commits:

### 1. Server-side apps → the shared client
The server code (chat tools, crons, migrations, bulk import, notifications,
operations, the file-index trigger, and the documents pipeline) did its engine
CRUD through the hand-rolled helpers in `core/server/aepbase.ts`.

- Adds `core/server/client.ts` — `serverClient(token, userId?)` constructs the
  shared client bound to the engine base (`AEPBASE_URL`) with a bearer-token
  strategy, plus `collectionAt()` for the alternating `[plural, id, …]` parent
  chains the chat executor builds dynamically.
- Migrates every consumer to it. Notable shape changes:
  - multipart create now rides a named `File` on the body (the client
    auto-assembles multipart; the engine already accepts per-field parts);
  - the classify trigger becomes an item-target `invoke('classify')`;
  - file downloads use `record.download(field)` (Blob, throws on error).
- Deletes the seven CRUD helpers (and the private `pathFor`/`aepError`/
  `ParentPath`) from `core/server/aepbase.ts`, which now keeps only the
  request-auth seam (`authenticate`, `aepbaseFetch`, `AEPBASE_URL`) that
  operates on a raw `Request`.

### 2. E2E helpers → the shared client
The e2e suite kept its own raw-`fetch` copies of the same `aep*` functions in
`tests/e2e/utils/aepbase-helpers.ts`, called by every spec and per-app
`e2e/helpers.ts`.

- Adds `e2eClient(token)` as the single seam; reimplements the domain helpers
  (`setAppFlag`, `createUser`, `deleteUsersExcept`, `createGroup`,
  `addGroupMember`, `postCustomMethod` via `client.raw()`) on it.
- Preserves the two load-bearing resilience behaviors the specs depend on:
  `listOrEmpty` returns `[]` on 403/404 (a denied user must see an empty list,
  not an exception), and `deleteIfPresent` swallows a 404 on delete.
- Migrates all 10 per-app `e2e/helpers.ts` and 17 specs; deletes the six aep*
  free functions. `tests/e2e` now depends on the client package.

## Test plan

- `make ci` (lint + type-check + build) — green.
- `make test`: 934 frontend vitest tests + 332 server/CLI Bun tests — pass.
  Affected unit tests reworked onto a shared fake client keyed by resolved
  engine path.
- `tests/e2e` type-checks clean (`tsc --noEmit`).
- Booted the real server (schema synced, migrations ran) and ran the pure-API
  permission-enforcement e2e suite — passes, exercising the 403 list-swallow,
  delete-if-present, and full client CRUD end to end.
- ⚠️ The full browser-driven e2e suite wasn't run in this environment (the
  sandbox's pre-installed Chromium build is mismatched with the pinned
  `@playwright/test` version, so `page.goto` navigation times out — unrelated
  to these changes). **Worth a full `make test-e2e` run in CI before merge** to
  confirm the UI-driven specs.

author: saud-alnasser
body:
Closes #223

Stacked: third of four, on top of #227.

## 🎯 Changes

`complex.name` is UNIQUE and the whole seed runs inside one transaction, so a single repeated name aborts the run and leaves **no database at all** — not a partial one. Names came from a bare `faker.location.street()`.

The issue called this a ceiling at roughly fifty complexes. It is not a ceiling — it is a coin flip at every count. Measured over 4,000 trials:

| complexes | P(seed aborts) |
| --- | --- |
| 10 (the committed count) | 0.75% |
| 50 | 16% |
| 100 | 51% |
| 200 | 95% |

So `pnpm db:seed` has always been able to fail; it simply had not yet.

The loop index is already unique, so it carries the guarantee rather than the generator's entropy. Four lines in `scripts/seed.ts`, inlined at the call site to match the `Room ${j + 1}` naming nine lines below rather than adding a helper.

`faker.helpers.uniqueArray` was the alternative and it works — tested to 200,000 without truncating. The index was chosen because it is unconditional and O(1), with no retry loop and no pool-exhaustion cliff.

**Verified by execution**, not by inspection: seeded 200, 500 and 2,000 complexes against throwaway databases; every run inserted the requested count with every name distinct.

**Left alone deliberately:** the same all-or-nothing failure exists on `tenant.phone`, whose 9 × 10⁷ space collides in **15.5% of runs at the committed 5,000 tenants** — twenty times this rate. #223's body asserts the opposite. Filed as #224 rather than folded in here, which would have made this diff unreviewable.

## ✅ Checklist

- [ ] I have added or updated the tests related to the changes made.

No test accompanies this, deliberately. The runner's glob is `src/**/*.test.mjs` and no test exists outside `src/`, so one placed beside the script would never run — widening the glob is a change to the test setup rather than to this bug. The fix is structural rather than statistical, so there is no flake to pin. Full suite green (220 pass, 0 fail), `svelte-check` 0 errors.

author: saud-alnasser
body:
Closes #222

Stacked: fourth of four, on top of #228.

## 🎯 Changes

ADR 0008 was accepted on a premise false in both halves: it has `data-view.svelte` backing four lists, and the tenant list rendering through `data-table.svelte` over a client-side query.

- **Five** modules import `data-view.svelte`, not four.
- `data-table.svelte` renders **none**. Its only importer is `tenant/component/table.svelte`, and that file has no importers at all — dead since the card-grid overhaul moved the tenants route away, after which it survived two relocation refactors that moved it without noticing.

**Two of 0008's three rejected alternatives depended on that second live implementation.** "Keep both" is void: there has only ever been one block, so its claim that the column vocabulary cannot be decided once was never true. "Extend `data-table`" is moot — a graveyard is not an implementation. Only "evolve `data-view` in place" survives, rejected for the one reason that never leaned on the premise: the replacement changes the data layer, the search and the virtualization at once, so what would survive is the filename, and a rewrite keeping the name cannot be diffed against what it replaced.

**The outcome is unchanged; the reasoning is not.** ADR 0009 restates the decision on correct facts and says that single argument *is* the single argument, rather than inheriting three. ADR 0008 moves to `superseded by 0009` with its prose untouched — a committed ADR's reasoning is frozen, and supersession is the only channel a correction has, which is why this is a new file rather than an edit.

**The map's two open decisions carried the same premise**, and one was load-bearing. Decision 03 pointed at the tenant table as a precedent to read, which would have walked the column-vocabulary decision into the same mistake; it now says to read it as history. Decision 04 asked which of two shipping models survives when only one ships. Both corrected in place — legal, because `ui-overhaul.md` is a map surface at `Status: mapping`, not a frozen spec.

**Dead code is not deleted here** — that is #225, cut and linked under #222. It also records that `design/primitive/data-table/` is *deliberately* kept unimported afterwards: `design/primitive/` is a generated catalogue where `empty` and `pagination` already sit unused, it wraps table-core into what the replacement needs, and regenerating one later is the operation ADR 0007 established is unsafe here.

## ✅ Checklist

- [ ] I have added or updated the tests related to the changes made.

No test surface — three documentation files, no executable code. Reviewed on both axes before commit; the review is what caught that #225 would have orphaned the `data-table` primitive.

author: pontusringblom
body:
## Symptom

The Academy Instructors Console has been down for individual organizations, reported six times and misdiagnosed as an authorization problem five of them. Proven against production at v1.0.219, `GET /api/academy/admin/summary` returns:

```
HTTP 500  failed to get test items: failed to decode test payload:
          uuid: incorrect UUID length 24 in string "corporate-sustainability"
```

A second failure sits on the same rows, on the learner-facing path:

```
Scan error on column index 6, name submission_data:
uuid: incorrect UUID length 2 in string "q1"
```

It looked like an authorization bug because it is per-organization - but only because only some organizations hold legacy records.

## Root cause

Identifier fields on the v1beta3 academy construct carried `format: uuid`, which makes oapi-codegen emit `uuid.UUID`. None of them identify a database row. They identify **Hugo content pages** and **content-authored quiz items**, whose values are opaque strings. `json.Unmarshal` fails on the first such record and aborts the whole response, so one bad row disables an entire endpoint.

The contradiction was visible in the schema itself: every one of these fields declared `maxLength: 500` alongside `format: uuid`, and a UUID is 36 characters.

The values only *look* like UUIDs today because `academy-theme` added `normalize-id.html`, which runs any non-UUID id through `derive-uuid.html` - a **sha1 digest reformatted into UUID shape**. That is a presentation coercion applied at build time, not an identity guarantee, and every payload persisted before it still holds the authored slug.

## What changed, and why each field

Producer evidence: `partial "id.html"` resolves to `.Params.id | default .RelPermalink` - an authored slug or a URL path. Real content carries `id: "conclusion"`, `id: "q1"`, `id: "a"`, even `id: "Spin Up a Kubernetes Cluster"`.

**Retyped to `string`** - content pages and content-authored items:

| Field | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `Quiz.id` | Hugo page id; front-matter `id`, else RelPermalink |
| `Parent.id` | one schema serving `parent`, `nextPage` and `prerequisites[]`, so all three are covered transitively |
| `Question.id` | authored in quiz front matter, e.g. `"q1"` |
| `QuestionOption.id` | authored in quiz front matter, e.g. `"a"` |
| `SubmittedAnswer.questionId` | must key-match `Question.id`; this is the `"q1"` scan error |
| `CurriculaCurrentItemData.id` | progress pointer at a content page; production holds slugs, full permalink URLs and the empty string |

**Deliberately left as `format: uuid`** - these are real database rows, each backed by a `uuid` Postgres column: `Quiz.orgId` (the theme emits the tenant UUID via `resolve-tenant.html`; its `example: meshery` was simply wrong and is corrected), every `userId` / `registrationId` / `testSessionId`, `AcademyRegistration.*` and `TestSubmission.*` core `Uuid` refs, `Certificate.orgId` / `recipientId`, and `UserRegistration.*`.

Each field was decided on evidence - what writes the value, and whether a `uuid` column sits behind it - not on the shape of its name.

## `Quiz.timeLimit`: both eras are real production data

This field is modelled as `oneOf: [integer, string]` because **no plain scalar can be correct**:

- `academy-theme` emits a **JSON number** - `int (or $p.timeLimit $p.time_limit 0)` in `partials/test/single.html` - and **all 149** currently built quiz `index.json` artifacts carry a number (`0, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40`);
- payloads persisted by earlier revisions hold a **string** - `"25"`, `"0"`, `"30"` and the non-numeric sentinel `"infinite"` - in **578 of 695** stored grade entries.

meshery-cloud unmarshals the built `index.json` straight into the canonical `Quiz` (`server/handlers/academy/quiz.go:196`). Typing the field as a string would therefore break **every live test-start**; leaving it an integer keeps failing the **578 stored rows**. The union is the honest modelling of a genuinely polymorphic field, not a hedge.

`QuizTimeLimit` (hand-written, same package) decodes either form. A string that does not parse to a positive number means "no time limit" and normalizes to `0` - the documented meaning of `0`, and what the UI already does (`parseInt`, then `NaN` or `<= 0` means no limit). It degrades rather than erroring **on purpose**: this construct was brought down by one unreadable record aborting a whole response. `MarshalJSON` always emits a number, so everything written from here on is canonical.

## Durability

Removing `format: uuid` alone left these fields tripping the validator's "ID property should have format: uuid" rule - **69 new advisory findings** that would have told the next contributor to add it straight back, restoring the outage. They now carry `x-id-format: external`, this repo's existing vocabulary for an identifier that is deliberately not a UUID. **Net new advisory findings: 0.**

## Verification

- `make validate-schemas`, `make consumer-audit`, `go build ./...`, `go test ./...`, `npm run build` - all pass.
- Generated Go shows `ID string` / `QuestionId string` for all six fields, and `TimeLimit QuizTimeLimit`.
- **73 real built quiz artifacts** decode into the canonical `Quiz`, alongside the historical `corporate-sustainability` / `"infinite"` payload and the `"q1"` submission. Regression tests cover both eras, using the exact payloads from the production errors.
- Strict-validation findings measured against the parent commit: **0 net new**.

## Wire compatibility

The six id fields are **wire-identical**: `format` steers only the Go generator here, so the generated TypeScript types and the RTK client change by **0 non-comment lines**. Only `AcademySchema.ts`, the JSON-schema mirror, moves - it drops 102 `"format": "uuid"` entries, which is the point of the change.

`Quiz.timeLimit` does change in TypeScript, from `number` to `number | string`. That is a widening to what consumers already receive and already handle.

## Scope left deliberately

`AcademyRegistration.contentId` is typed `uuid.UUID` against a `content_id text NOT NULL` column that joins to `academy_curricula.id text`. **Same defect class, not yet triggered** - it will fire the first time a pre-normalization registration is decoded. Left out to keep this change proportional; it wants its own fix.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **New Features**
  - Academy content identifiers now support opaque, content-authored strings instead of requiring UUIDs.
  - Quiz time limits accept numeric or string values, including legacy formats.
  - Invalid, non-positive, or unlimited time-limit values are normalized consistently and returned canonically as numbers.

- **Compatibility**
  - Historical quizzes and submissions with slug-based or non-UUID identifiers continue to decode successfully.

- **Documentation**
  - Added schema guidance for external content IDs, polymorphic fields, and JSON/database tag casing.

# Backport

This will backport the following commits from `main` to `9.4`:
 - [[ResponseOps] ES Query grouping results in odd group fields in alert (#280872)](https://github.com/elastic/kibana/pull/280872)

<!--- Backport version: 9.6.6 -->

### Questions ?
Please refer to the [Backport tool documentation](https://github.com/sorenlouv/backport)

<!--BACKPORT [{"author":{"name":"Alexi Doak","email":"109488926+doakalexi@users.noreply.github.com"},"sourceCommit":{"committedDate":"2026-08-03T19:55:17Z","message":"[ResponseOps] ES Query grouping results in odd group fields in alert (#280872)

Resolves https://github.com/elastic/kibana/issues/272553


## Summary

This PR resolves 2 bugs related to the ES query ES|QL rule grouping.

Bug 1 - INLINE STATS ... BY :
The ES|QL grouping logic didn't account for INLINE STATS ... BY so every
column was treated as a grouping field instead of just the BY fields.


Bug 2 - AlertId / Grouping in `parse_aggregation_results.ts`
This is the case where we dropped null/undefined values for the grouping
AlertId the grouping field names were reported as the full, unfiltered
list. The grouping parser in `parse_aggregation_results.ts` zips the
field names to values positionally, so when they aren't the same length
from dropping the null/undefined fields, every later value was written
to the wrong field name, causing `kibana.alert.grouping` to be wrong. To
fix this, we now pass in the correct field names `keyFields` for each
bucket, and the grouping parser checks for `keyFields` and falls back to
`termField`. The AlertId logic stays the same, we just now are ensuring
we're creating the grouping object with the right name/values.



### Checklist


- [ ] [Unit or functional
tests](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/kibana/master/development-tests.html)
were updated or added to match the most common scenarios

### To verify
Bug 1:
1. Create an ES|QL ES query rule with `INLINE STATS ... BY` and "Create
an alert for each row" selected.
ex. `FROM .kibana-event-log* | INLINE STATS host.uptime =
SUM(event.duration) BY event.provider, event.action | LIMIT 1`
2. Let the rule run and create alerts and go to Dev Tools to verify the
alert documents by running the query below:
```
GET .internal.alerts-stack.alerts-default-*/_search
```
3. Verify that `kibana.alert.grouping` contains only the BY fields with
correct values, `{ event: { provider: ..., action: ... } }` and verify
that the `kibana.alert.instance.id` contains the values from
event.provider and event.action.

Bug 2:

1. Create an ES|QL ES query rule where a leading grouping field is null
for some rows and select and "Create an alert for each row".
ex. `FROM .kibana-event-log* | EVAL maybe = CASE(event.action ==
"new-instance", event.action, null) | STATS c = COUNT(*) BY maybe,
event.provider | WHERE c > 0`
2. Let the rule run and create alerts and go to Dev Tools to verify the
alert documents by running the query below:
```
GET .internal.alerts-stack.alerts-default-*/_search
```
3. Verify that alerts with the null first field still map their
remaining values to the correct field name in `kibana.alert.grouping`
and and verify that the `kibana.alert.instance.id` looks as expected.

author: j4rvisstant
body:
Prepares the 0.7.1 release: version bump plus the changelog roll. No code changes and no behaviour changes. Not tagged, not published.

## What 0.7.1 contains

This release mostly repairs things that claimed to work. `reset_target` never reached the target on the documented OpenOCD backend, in any of its three modes: it sent a command that does not exist until `init` has run, and the abort was then recorded as an unconfirmed hardware state, so a board OpenOCD had never addressed took the bench out of service until a person inspected it. The deny rules `setup` writes protected nothing on either platform — one form the host accepts and never consults, warning about it at every start, the other anchored at the settings file rather than at the filesystem root, which was the worse half for being silent. An upgrade destroyed the installation outright while an agent host held it open, which is the state anyone following the documented way to add `[pyocd]` or `[can]` was in. pyOCD's real "target type not recognized" message matched none of the phrases the classifier looked for, so the catalogue entry naming the CMSIS pack commands never fired on the one message that should produce it. What is new points the same way: `doctor` names the Windows application package whose grant got a path refused and asks whether a target is supported before a flash discovers it is not, and the quickstart names the Linux install obstacles instead of leaving the next reader to find them.

Fifteen `[Unreleased]` entries roll into `[0.7.1]` — 2 Added, 6 Changed, 7 Fixed — unchanged in wording. In rough order of weight:

- `reset_target` sent `reset <mode>` to an OpenOCD that had not run `init`, so the interpreter answered `invalid command name "reset"` and the run ended before the probe was opened. `run`, `halt` and `init` alike, on the documented default backend. Fixes hardci-hq#83.
- That abort was reported as an unconfirmed hardware state, so it quarantined the bench — and the automatic settle ran into the same missing `init`. A rejected command is now told apart from an unconfirmed outcome and returns `debugger_command_rejected` with `target_contacted: false`, `side_effect_status: "not_started"` and no quarantine.
- The deny rules `setup --agent claude-code` writes are now the ones Claude Code reads: one filesystem-anchored `Edit(//…)` rule per protected tree, with the superseded `Write(…)` and single-slash forms taken back on a repeat run. Fixes hardci-hq#81.
- `agentic-hil upgrade` refuses with `installation_in_use` before removing anything when a process is running out of the installation it would replace, naming each holder by pid and image path. Previously the delete failed on Windows and left no installation at all — neither the old one nor the new one.
- An upgrade through `pip` or `uv pip` keeps `[can]` and `[pyocd]` instead of resolving them away.
- pyOCD's actual `Target type <name> not recognized` message now reaches the `target_type_invalid:pyocd` remediation, with the message pinned verbatim by a regression test.
- `unsafe_configured_path` carries `untrusted_principals`, naming the Windows application package behind a capability SID rather than only the SID. Implements hardci-hq#64.
- `doctor` reports `debuggers.<name>.target_support`, keeping `unsupported`, `undetermined` and `not_applicable` apart. Implements hardci-hq#66.
- `AI_AGENT_QUICKSTART.md` names the PEP 668 and TLS-interception dead ends by the error text a reader matches on, and announces the approval `setup` needs before the command rather than after the refusal.
- The OpenOCD test fake now keeps OpenOCD's two stages, so a command line nothing could execute fails the suite — which is what let the `reset` defect ship.
- Machine-read JSON goes out compact; the `tools/call` text block is now byte-identical to `structuredContent`.

## Version bump

Every position `python tools/check_version_consistency.py --list` reports now says `0.7.1` — 12 files, 19 occurrences. The check is silent and the uncovered-file sweep flagged nothing.

One occurrence the check does not enforce was bumped with them: the `uvx --from git+…@v0.7.0` repository-check line in `TROUBLESHOOTING.md`. It sits in a file `locations()` already covers, so the sweep skips it, and `_requirement_pins` matches only `>=` and `==`, so nothing would have caught it left behind. Every previous release bumped it by hand.

`[0.7.0]` and everything below it in `CHANGELOG.md` is byte-identical to `master`: the changelog diff is four inserted lines above that heading and nothing else.

## Verification

- `ruff check src tests evals tools` clean; `ruff check examples` clean.
- `python tools/check_shipped_references.py` clean.
- `python tools/check_version_consistency.py .` silent.
- `python -m build` plus `twine check dist/*` — both distributions pass.
- Full suite on Windows with `APPDATA`/`LOCALAPPDATA` redirected out of the real profile; the only failures are this machine's known ACL-dependent group, unchanged from `master`.

author: studiahub
body:
## Qué

El sync LMS → WC ahora fuerza **Virtual + Descargable** en el producto del curso, tanto al crearlo como en cada sincronización posterior.

## Por qué

WooCommerce solo cierra una orden automáticamente al cobrar si **todos** sus line items son virtual **y** downloadable. El connector seteaba `set_virtual(true)` solo en `create_product`, y `downloadable` no lo seteaba nunca.

Resultado: tildar "Descargable" quedaba como paso manual del admin. Si se lo olvidaba, la orden moría en `processing`, el webhook nunca veía `completed` y el alumno pagaba sin quedar inscripto — el clásico "pagué y no entré", que falla en silencio.

## Detalle

Forzarlo también en `update_product` es deliberado y es la parte importante: es una excepción a la regla de no tocar `status`/`visibility`/`stock`/`sku` (esos sí son preferencia del admin). Virtual + downloadable no es preferencia, es requisito para cobrar — y así **repara los productos ya rotos** en el próximo sync, sin que nadie toque nada.

No hace falta adjuntar ningún archivo: la casilla sola alcanza para que WC cierre el pedido.

## Ojo

- Esto **no llega a los WordPress de los clientes** hasta cortar release (bump de versión + `bin/release.sh`).
- Edge case conocido: un curso que incluyera materiales físicos con envío no debería ser virtual. Hoy se fuerza igual. No hay ningún cliente en esa situación.

author: wgu9
body:
Partially addresses #436. JSON support remains out of scope for this PR.

## What changed

Generic `.yml` / `.yaml` files now produce value-free, path-addressable graph
structure:

- aggregated `YamlPath` nodes for mappings and repeated sequence shapes
- occurrence counts plus bounded source-line/range samples
- mapping-scoped duplicate-key diagnostics with exact line samples
- canonical `CONTAINS` edges and `REFERENCES` edges for aliases/merge keys
- distinct reference targets for typed and duplicate anchored definitions
- `changed_yaml_paths` in change/review output
- CLI kind filtering, safe graph serialization, visualization, and docs support

Scalar values are deliberately discarded. The graph stores structural key paths
and YAML types, not configuration values. Query, search, and change-analysis
responses share the same nested `yaml` metadata contract.

## Safety and compatibility

This incorporates the earlier YAML review feedback from #539, #577, and #462:

- malformed or pathologically recursive YAML fails safely
- aliases, root/self aliases, merge sequences, and complex mapping keys have
  regression coverage
- per-file limits bound node count, nesting depth, exact/schema/identity path
  length, and diagnostic samples
- repeated sequence shapes aggregate under `[*]` paths
- existing Ansible and Spring parsers retain precedence
- files rejected by a specialized path heuristic fall back to generic YAML
- full-build/query coverage asserts zero dangling YAML edges

## How this differs from earlier attempts

| Earlier review concern | This PR |
|---|---|
| Bare or dangling graph endpoints | Canonical persisted identities plus full-build dangling-edge assertions |
| Raw configuration values in metadata | Values are never stored |
| Framework- or organization-specific YAML schema | Generic structural paths and YAML types |
| One node per repeated list item | Aggregated `[*]` schema paths with bounded occurrence samples |
| Missing malformed/cycle/size handling | Error, recursion, node, depth, path, and metadata bounds |
| Parser-only coverage | Persistence, query, change analysis, visualization, and specialization regressions |

## Verification

Verification uses only synthetic fixtures and this public project's test suite:

- Full suite: **2,413 passed, 7 skipped, 2 xpassed**
- Focused YAML/change/incremental suite: **158 passed**
- Ruff (source and changed tests): **clean**
- Mypy (same flags as CI): **clean**
- `git diff --check`: **clean**

```bash
uv run --python 3.13 pytest tests/ --tb=short -q
uv run pytest tests/test_yaml_parser.py tests/test_changes.py \
  tests/test_incremental.py -q --tb=short
uv run ruff check code_review_graph/
uv run mypy code_review_graph/ --ignore-missing-imports --no-strict-optional
```

The synthetic coverage includes persisted graph queries, zero dangling YAML
edges, scalar-value absence, malformed and recursive input, oversized paths,
duplicate keys, aliases, merges, multi-document YAML, and Spring/Ansible
precedence.

## Deliberate non-goals

This first phase does not add JSON indexing, scalar-value indexing,
duplicate-value detection, cross-file business-rule validation, business-owner
inference, or Helm values-to-template resolution (#199). Those require explicit
policy and privacy semantics on top of structural indexing.

author: filipeforattini
body: Closes #3201. ADR 0098 was written from a single-CLI-session perspective and no longer described the three-layer reality: a host-scoped daemon, a per-project Worker, and the dispatching session. A reader looking for "where is the worker log" had to guess between the worker directory and `.red/tmp/logs//`, and nothing said that daemon state belongs outside a project's `.red/` at all. The amendment separates the three owners and says why each boundary exists — notably that the daemon outlives every project and is shared by all of them, so a per-project home would make one project's cleanup delete another's evidence. `apps/dev/tests/lane-taxonomy-docs.test.ts` pins the taxonomy so the doc and the tree cannot drift apart silently. --- **Opened by hand.** The dispatched Worker completed the work and pushed all five commits, then exited 1 without opening a PR: ``` [afk] orphaned work: afk/3201-… (#3201) — 5 commits ahead of the base, no open pull request [afk] dispatch left work with no route to main: … — exiting 1 ``` The engine detected the orphan and reported it accurately rather than claiming success — that part worked. What is missing is the route: finished, pushed work with no PR is invisible to every surface that reads PRs, and it is one `git gc` away from being lost. Filed separately as the defect; this PR is the recovery. --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Autofix is disabled.
